I've been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when the company launched its T-Mobile ONE plan. Throughout my time with T-Mobile, I've always had the military discount, but even with that discount, my monthly bill eventually ballooned to $113 thanks to T-Mobile price hikes. I decided enough was enough and started looking for cheaper alternatives. Combined with the fact that Apple's iPhone 18 Pro costs at least $100 more this year, I figured that if I was going to get a new phone anyway, cutting my monthly cell phone bill might help offset the cost. So I started researching Mobile Virtual Network Operators (MVNOs).

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." Simply put, an MVNO is a wireless service provider that doesn't operate its own nationwide cellular network. Instead, they purchase network access from one of the major carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon) and resell the service to their own customers. Think of them as wireless middlemen.

This means switching to an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up the network you're currently using. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's network, and US Mobile lets customers choose between the big three. This article will focus on these three MVNOs because they were the three I researched most heavily before leaving T-Mobile, but there are other options out there as well.

The short version is that MVNOs give you another way to purchase cellular service without going directly to the company that owns the network.

Why Are MVNOs Cheaper, and What's the "Catch?"

If MVNOs can use the same AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon cellular networks, how can they charge so much less? The short answer is that MVNOs don't carry all of the costs of running a nationwide wireless carrier. They don't have to build and maintain the network, many of them operate primarily online rather than maintaining physical retail stores, and they have fewer employees. These savings can be passed on to customers in the form of lower monthly bills.

MVNO plans also tend to be simpler, without a lot of the "perks" and extras you'd find with traditional wireless carriers. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get a free streaming service or other perks designed to keep you loyal to a major carrier. But if you actually want those "free" perks, the savings from using an MVNO would more than cover the cost of paying for them yourself.

This situation applies perfectly to me. I always looked forward to the free MLB.TV subscription that came with T-Mobile and used it every season, but I never watch Netflix, so the "free Netflix" perk is completely wasted on me. Even if I wanted both services, I could pay for them myself and still come out ahead with what I save by switching to an MVNO. At the end of the day, I mainly just want reliable, affordable cellular service—I don't need T-Mobile to throw in a bunch of extras.

The "catch" isn't necessarily worse service—it's that you're paying for less. What exactly you're giving up depends on which MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming might be limited to lower resolutions, high-speed or premium data amounts might differ, and network priority might be different. I have extremely fast Wi-Fi at home, and I'm rarely in "congested" environments like concerts or stadiums, so network priority doesn't matter much to me in my day-to-day use. But I do travel internationally occasionally, so international data is an important consideration. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others charge extra or offer more limited coverage when traveling outside the U.S.

There are also some less obvious differences, particularly when it comes to buying a new iPhone. When you choose an MVNO as your carrier, Apple Card Monthly Installments and the iPhone Upgrade Program are not available. If you want to use either of those options, you're limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. In practice, this means if you buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you'll typically have to pay for it all at once. Major carriers also offer generous trade-in credits and other promotions that typically aren't available with MVNOs. Apple Watch support also isn't universal, so if you use a cellular Apple Watch, this is something to keep in mind.

Finally, most MVNOs rely primarily on phone and online support rather than physical stores with staff you can talk to face-to-face. I consider myself tech-savvy and have no desire to stand in line at a store waiting for help. In my experience, the salespeople in stores end up calling the same support lines and getting put on hold just like I would if I called from home, so this isn't a barrier for me.

It's important to note that these limitations aren't universal across all MVNOs. They vary by carrier and plan, so it's worth understanding exactly what you're getting before you switch.

Three MVNOs Worth Considering

After making the decision to leave T-Mobile, I started looking for alternatives. Verizon and AT&T's postpaid plans were more expensive than what I was already paying, so the other two major carriers were non-starters for me. I ultimately narrowed my search down to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something that appealed to me, and all three would allow me to significantly cut my wireless bill without sacrificing the use of a major carrier's network.

US Mobile is the most flexible of the three, and it's the carrier I ultimately chose when I switched from T-Mobile. That doesn't necessarily mean it's the best fit for you, or even that it's the best MVNO of the three. It just happened to be the one that fit me best.

In fact, US Mobile wasn't my first choice. I had never even heard of the company before I started researching MVNOs. But the more I learned about what it offered, the more it stood out. Here's why: US Mobile offers service on all three major networks, letting customers choose whichever network works best for them. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on that lets you activate two networks on the same iPhone at the same time without needing a second phone number. Both networks are tied to the same line, and your iPhone can use whichever network has the better signal for calls and data. For example, if T-Mobile's network is great at your office but Verizon is better at home, you could take advantage of both without carrying two phones or managing two numbers. US Mobile charges extra for this feature, and I don't need it myself, but it's nice that the option is there.

After recently moving, I wanted to see how Verizon's coverage compared to T-Mobile's near our new home, so I decided to test both networks at once. I set my wife's iPhone on US Mobile's Light Speed network (that's T-Mobile) and mine on Warp (that's Verizon) so we could compare coverage firsthand. The end result showed that Verizon was significantly better in our area, so switching to US Mobile was a win-win: better coverage and a much lower monthly bill.

Mint Mobile was originally my first choice because it's owned by T-Mobile, meaning I could stay on the network I was familiar with while paying less. What I didn't like was that it doesn't include international data. My wife and I enjoy cruise vacations, and international travel is a part of our lives, so being able to use cellular data outside the U.S. is important to us. Mint does offer international data, but it's an extra cost that would quickly eat into some of the savings. I also didn't like that taxes and fees were charged separately.

Visible is also simple and straightforward, but it only uses Verizon's network. My biggest hesitation with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. I've been on T-Mobile for nearly a decade and know its network performance like the back of my hand, but I had no idea how Verizon's coverage would compare. That was really the only thing that kept me from choosing Visible over US Mobile, because US Mobile gave me the opportunity to try Verizon's network while still having T-Mobile and AT&T available if Verizon didn't work out. Visible also offers a free cellular Apple Watch plan with its top-tier unlimited data plan, which was another appealing feature. (US Mobile offers the same perk on its top-tier plan when using Warp, which is Verizon's network.)

What You Need to Switch Carriers

Switching to an MVNO was easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and it took about ten minutes to transfer both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile. I didn't even have to get off the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, but this article will focus on iPhone), and your existing carrier account information. If you want to keep your number, make sure you don't cancel your existing service until the number transfer is complete.

Here's what you need to switch carriers:

  • Your existing wireless carrier account number
  • Transfer PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I prepaid for a year of US Mobile's two unlimited data plans in advance to make the switch. My wife doesn't have a cellular Apple Watch and doesn't care about higher-quality video, so she went with US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, which is $100 cheaper than the Unlimited Premium plan I chose. Both lines, including the Apple Watch plan, came to $500 for the year, compared to the $1,356 per year I was paying T-Mobile for two lines without Apple Watch service. (Again, that was with the military discount already applied.)

Generating a transfer PIN through T-Mobile was straightforward—I expected it to be more hidden or complicated than it was. Instructions for doing the same with Verizon and AT&T are also included.

Once the iPhones were connected to Wi-Fi, US Mobile emailed me the new eSIMs, and installation was just a matter of tapping a button in the email and following the on-screen prompts. My wife's iPhone was the same process. The only extra step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I was able to do easily through US Mobile's app.

Why I'm Sticking with an MVNO

Same coverage, lower cost: For the money I'm saving, the trade-offs I've made are absolutely worth it. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so cellular data isn't the most important thing to me (though in speed tests, US Mobile is just as fast as T-Mobile was). What matters most is having a strong, reliable cellular signal when I'm away from Wi-Fi, especially for making and receiving calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have done away with traditional contract plans in favor of device installment plans, which achieve the same effect by requiring you to stay with their network until your phone is paid off. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I want the freedom that comes with having an unlocked phone, but I was also happy to see that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible don't have contract requirements.

Easy and convenient to switch carriers: Most MVNOs let you pay month-to-month, so you're not locked into a long-term contract. If one carrier has a great deal one month and another has a better deal the next, switching is quick and easy. Prepaid accounts also don't require a credit check, meaning every time a carrier pulls your credit it won't ding your credit score the way it would with a postpaid account, and you won't be denied based on your credit history. My credit is good, but I still don't want a hard inquiry on my credit report just because I decided to switch from T-Mobile to Verizon.

Zach Chadwick's Top Comment

I've been on T-Mobile since 2014. Two lines with device trade-in promotional discounts were $135 per month. After price hikes, new plans, and trade-in requirements, it went up to $185 per month.

I switched to Visible in September 2025. I chose the Pro plan and used the promo code SAVE26 to get their best plan for $33 per month for 26 months.

When my mom's trade-in credits ended, I moved her plan over to Visible as well. They had a half-off promotion on their best plan with annual prepayment at the time. So her service for the year was just $275.

This year, the total for both lines came to $671. That's the equivalent of four months of service with T-Mobile.

I haven't had any issues so far. I've turned on autopay. They don't require a debit card or checking account. I'm on 5G UW 90% of the time. I can also stream 4K video with no buffering or lag.

I've also created a Visible "Circle" where I can invite others and get $5 per month back per line, which lets me cover the cost for everyone in my Circle.

More savings with annual prepayment: As a trade-off for flexibility, if you're willing to prepay for a year of service, you can usually save even more. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts on annual plans, so you'll be giving up some of the freedom to switch carriers at any time in exchange for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I enjoy cruises. If you've ever forgotten to switch your iPhone to airplane mode on a ship and let it connect to the ship's cellular network, you know the shock—and potentially astronomical bill—that follows. With a prepaid plan, I don't have to worry about accidentally racking up massive roaming charges. If the plan doesn't include international roaming, my phone simply won't connect to a foreign network and charge me for it. US Mobile's plans include taxes and fees, so the price listed is the price you actually pay.

Switching to an MVNO isn't just about finding the cheapest service—it's about getting what you want without paying for a bunch of stuff you don't need. So far, I don't feel like I'm missing out on anything that matters to me (though I'll definitely miss the free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I now have an extra Apple Watch line that I didn't have before, and I'm paying less. I kept the same iPhone, kept the same phone number, US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network coverage is actually better in my area, and if a better option comes along in the future, I have the freedom to switch again.

Your priorities might be different from mine, and MVNOs might not be for everyone. But if you're paying a lot for wireless service and haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth a look. You might be surprised at how little you actually have to give up.
